newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel court considers petitions against Netanyahu.
newsitem.headline: Israel court considers petitions against Netanyahu.

text.p: Israel High Court judges considered requests on Wednesday by opposition legislators to order Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's indictment for fraud and breach of trust.
The petitions marked Netanyahu's second bout with an affair state attorneys have said raised "real suspicions" of corruption against him and his justice minister but did not warrant prosecuting them.

Earlier on Wednesday, a five-judge panel threw out related petitions including a request to order a state investigation into the allegations and one to make public a 995-page police report on the affair.
"As far as we can judge the situation, the prime minister committed crimes and should be indicted," said parliament member Yossi Sarid of the left-wing Meretz party.

Police recommended last month that both Netanyahu and Justice Minister Tzachi Hanegbi be charged with fraud and breach of trust in the ill-fated appointment of lawyer Roni Bar-On as attorney-general last January.

But state prosecutors said there was sufficient evidence to indict only one figure in the affair, key coalition legislator Aryeh Deri of the religious Shas party, prompting charges of racism by Shas's mainly blue-collar Sephardi constituency.
"This is part of the Ashkenazi establishment's campaign against the Sephardis," said attorney Dan Kochavi in court on Wednesday during a dramatic moment in the proceedings.
Judges turned down his request to repeal Deri's indictment.

Sephardis are Jews of North African and Middle Eastern origin. Ashkenazis are Jews who immigrated to Israel from European countries. Sephardi Jews have long complained of discrimination in a country dominated by Ashkenazi elites.
Israel's Channel One Television alleged Bar-On's appointment as attorney-general was part of a deal to win a plea bargain for Deri in his three-year corruption trial. Deri has denied it.
Bar-On, who quit 12 hours after taking office amid a public outcry that he was unqualified for the job, was cleared by prosecutors.
Three state prosecutors defended their position in Wednesday's hearing.
"The state drafted a 50-page response to all the petitions," said Justice Ministry spokewoman Etty Eshed.
Netanyahu, 47, said in a televised speech last month the report issued by prosecutors cleared him of any wrongdoing.

The results of the three-month police investigation prompted members of Netanyahu's own government to call for the dismissal of Hanegbi as the country's overseer of justice but the prime minister's coalition has remained intact.
"The bottom line is I didn't commit any crime and the attorney-general confirmed that," Netanyahu said last month.
He apologised for any mistakes in the January appointment, but accused the media and opposition of trying to use the affair "to overthrow the government".
Earlier this week Netanyahu announced he would not sack Hanegbi, 40, concluding he was still fit for the job.
Some political analysts had speculated Hanegbi would be shuffled out of the Justice Ministry if his predecessor Yaakov Neeman was cleared this week of obstructing justice and lying to judges.
Neeman, who stepped down last August after being indicted, will hear the verdict in his own case on Thursday.
